source.title: A Unified Theory of Sparse Dictionary Learning in Mechanistic Interpretability: Piecewise Biconvexity and Spurious Minima
source.authors: Yi-Ming Tang; Harshvardhan Saini; Zhao-Qian Yao; Zheng Lin; Yi-Zhen Liao; Jing-Yi Cui; Yi-Sen Wang; Mengnan Du; Dian-Bo Liu

record.tranche_reason: The paper gives theoretical results that refine the clean-feature picture by showing that hierarchical concepts can admit absorption patterns and that polysemantic patterns can be partial minima. It does not compare SAE dictionary sizes.
record.gate_note: The paper's own theoretical results on feature absorption and polysemantic partial minima bear on the claim. Its feature-recovery experiments concern feature anchoring, not feature splitting, so they are excluded. Discussion of splitting and absorption results from other work is cited background, not a result of this study.
record.test_reason: Theorem 3.8 is the study's own result on V4. It constructs a realizable SDL activation pattern in which one sub-concept gets a dedicated neuron and the parent neuron stops responding to it. It is a theoretical existence result, not a measurement on trained SAEs. No experiment measures splitting or absorption.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct, with one qualification. The authors conclude that hierarchical concept structures naturally induce realizable absorption patterns, and say these manifest as partial minima. The formal result proves realizability only; the partial-minimum link is asserted from Theorem 3.6 rather than proved for the absorption pattern.
record.recipe_differences: The study provides a theoretical analysis of SDL optimization and absorption patterns; it does not train and compare SAEs at increasing dictionary sizes.

fits_no_version.finding: Every realizable polysemantic activation pattern that partitions the ground-truth features has a partial minimum with positive loss (Theorem 3.6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SDL objectives have pervasive spurious polysemantic partial minima under the linear representation hypothesis.

record.problems: The relevant absorption result is theoretical and establishes realizability, not that gradient-based training reaches the pattern or how often trained SAEs exhibit it. The analysis relies on representation assumptions, including extreme sparsity for some results, and the paper notes these assumptions may not hold in real neural networks.
record.rows_left_out: Feature-anchoring recovery results and the Llama resampling loss comparison do not measure feature splitting or absorption. No rows were omitted for the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: No dictionary-size sweep and no comparison of coarse and fine features.
No splitting analysis in large models or open SAE releases. The Llama 3.1 8B run reports only loss with and without resampling.
No measurement of nested families, geometric closeness, or correspondence to a concept hierarchy.

Untested: empirical prevalence of absorption in trained SAEs, and whether changing dictionary size or sparsity fixes it. The partial-minimum property of the absorption pattern is asserted, not proved.
No comparison of latents across SAE sizes and no measure of novel latents.

The paper attributes pathologies to the SDL optimization landscape, but does not test splitting as an artifact of the objective. Its Matryoshka SAE results concern ground-truth recovery, not splitting.

record.verdict_notes: Of the paper's results, only Theorem 3.8 bears on V4. The proof of Theorem 3.8 uses a threshold c > 0, which differs from the zero-threshold realizability used for Theorem 3.6. The two results therefore connect only loosely. Ground-truth features are assumed independent and, for several results, extremely sparse; the authors flag both as limitations. The feature-anchoring experiments (Tables 1, 2, 4–7), the CLIP qualitative examples and the resampling run do not measure splitting or absorption. They are correctly left out of the rows.

versions.untested_parts: No sweep over dictionary sizes or comparison of coarse and finer features.
No large-model or open-release SAE comparison of splitting.
No measurement of nested feature families, geometric closeness, or correspondence to a conceptual hierarchy.

The paper proves that an absorption pattern is realizable under a hierarchical feature structure; it does not empirically test trained SAE firing, absorption prevalence, or whether changing dictionary size or sparsity fixes it.
No comparison of latents across SAE dictionary sizes or measurement of novel larger-dictionary latents.
The paper analyzes SDL optimization and hierarchy-related absorption, but does not test splitting as an objective artifact or compare objectives such as Matryoshka SAEs on splitting.

rows.subject: Sparse Dictionary Learning (theoretical framework)
rows.size_stated: nq = M + 1 in the constructed activation pattern
rows.operation_detail: Proves that a hierarchical parent feature's activation set can be partitioned by separating one sub-concept into its own neuron.

conditions.value: parent concepts decompose into at least two sub-concepts
the original parent activation pattern is realizable

rows.measure: Realizability of an absorption activation pattern
rows.value: Theorem 3.8 states that for each parent, a realizable pattern can be changed so one sub-concept has a dedicated neuron while the parent neuron responds to the remaining sub-concepts.
rows.note: This is a theoretical existence result, not an empirical observation that trained SAEs exhibit the pattern.
rows.check: Theoretical construction, not an observation. It shows the absorption pattern is realizable, assuming thresholded activation and maximum interference M < 1. It does not prove that the specific P′ is a partial minimum; that link to Theorem 3.6 is only asserted in the text. It does not show the pattern arises in training or survives changes in dictionary size or sparsity. The subject is an abstract SDL framework, not a trained SAE. Baseline: not applicable.

relation.reason: Theorem 3.8 is the study's own result on absorption, bearing on V4 for realizability only.

tranche.reason: Theorem 3.8 is a specific formal argument that SDL can realize a pattern where a parent neuron loses a sub-concept to a dedicated neuron. It supports the challenge version V4, so clean splitting into hierarchies (V1/V3) needs restating. That fits T5.

source_check.notes: Theory only for absorption. The Llama 3.1 8B SAE runs test neuron resampling, not absorption. The text overloads M: it is both the number of parents (the encoder has M+1 rows) and the maximum interference (< 1, used in the proof only). The proof also applies one new threshold c'' to every row and does not check that the other parents' sets are preserved.

statements.problem: None for this study. It says only that Theorem 3.8 shows an absorption pattern is realizable, and the 'why' adds the limit (realizability, not occurrence). The group heading 'favours or stabilises' matches how the authors frame it: absorption patterns 'manifest as partial minima'.
